newsitem.title: IVORY COAST: Tight security for violence-delayed Ivorian polls.
newsitem.headline: Tight security for violence-delayed Ivorian polls.

text.p: Ivory Coast wrapped up its second multi-party elections on Sunday with parliamentary by-elections under tight security in this opposition stronghold where political and ethnic violence prevented polling in 1995.

Eighteen candidates were contesting eight of the national assembly's 175 seats around the Ivorian Popular Front (FPI) stronghold of Gagnoa in the centre west cocoa growing area and in three constituencies in the north and east.
The results will have little impact on parliament where President Henri Konan Bedie's supporters have a huge majority.

"No incident has been brought to our attention at this time," Interior Minister Emile Constant Bombet told state television half-way through the poll, noting that problems traditionally arose just before polling ended.
He estimated turnout at about 35 percent.
Ivory Coast, the world's top cocoa producer, held its first multi-party elections in 1990 after independence president Felix Houphouet-Boigny bowed to pressure for democratic reform.

Soldiers, police and paramilitary gendarmes conducted spot checks and guarded polling stations on Sunday in the Gagnoa area, where the West African nation's November 1995 parliamentary poll was postponed because of violence.

"Don't react to provocation," FPI leader Laurent Gbagbo, who spearheaded the 1990 campaign for multi-party politics and is trying to regain the Ouragahio seat he held in the previous parliament, told his supporters.
As a gesture of reconciliation, he offered a ram to the general secretary of Bedie's Democratic Party (PDCI) Laurent Dona Fologo, who was touring the Gagnoa region.
The interior ministry, which runs elections in Ivory Coast, postponed polling in the Gagnoa area because of bloodshed during the October 1995 presidential election.
Clashes between indigenous Bete supporters of Gbagbo's party and migrant farmers of Bedie's Baoule tribe killed 25 people and triggered a Baoule exodus. Most of the dead were Baoule.
Gbagbo and his allies in the main opposition had boycotted the presidential poll and their supporters disrupted polling in Gagnoa and elsewhere. The death toll nationwide was 35.
In the November parliamentary poll, Bedie's party won 146 seats, the Rally of the Republicans (RDR) formed by Democratic Party dissidents won 14 and Gbagbo's party eight.

Reruns in Seguela in the north and Adzope in the east follow the scrapping of original results following problems. A rerun in Korhogo in the north followed the death of the elected RDR member. Four districts held municipal reruns on Sunday.
